alt: Six stages: Companions learning in the Prophet's lifetime, mainly by memory; Companions teaching across new cities after 632; Successors travelling and keeping notebooks; the first official collection ordered by Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz (717–720); musannaf and musnad collections; and the sahih and sunan collections of the third Islamic century.
caption: Six stages, from memory to strictly selected collections; the official order of 717–720 is the turning point.

alt: Two panels. A musannaf arranges Hadiths by subject, such as purification, prayer and zakat; al-Muwatta of Imam Malik is the example, useful for finding rulings. A musnad arranges them by the narrating Companion, such as all of Abu Bakr's narrations; the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal is the example, easier for checking chains but harder for finding rulings.
caption: Musannaf: by subject. Musnad: by narrator.

after: ## Stage 6: the sahih and sunan collections
alt: The six Sunni collections. Highlighted together as al-Sahihayn: al-Bukhari (d. 870), with the strictest conditions, and Muslim (d. 875), which gathers all versions of a Hadith in one place. Below: Abu Dawud, focused on legal rulings; al-Tirmidhi, commenting on grades and legal views; al-Nasa'i, careful about narrators; and Ibn Majah, with Hadiths not in the other five.
caption: Know one main feature for each of the six books; al-Bukhari and Muslim rank highest.

alt: Two checklists. Isnad tests: good character ('adala), accurate memory (dabt) and an unbroken chain, checked in biographical dictionaries. Matn tests: no contradiction of the Qur'an or established Sunna, nothing against reason or known history, and the Prophet's way of speaking. Hadiths are graded sahih, hasan, da'if or mawdu'; only sahih and hasan establish rulings.
caption: Chain and text are both tested; only sahih and hasan Hadiths are used for rulings.

alt: Three rows link a Qur'anic command to the detail supplied by the Hadiths: prayer, whose times, units and actions come from the Sunna; zakat, whose rates and minimum amounts come from the Hadiths; and cases where the Qur'an is silent, such as the ban on gold and silk clothing for men. Cards add ijma', qiyas and Sura 59.7.
caption: Without the Hadiths, Qur'anic commands such as prayer and zakat could not be carried out.

alt: Six steps for a 10-mark answer: define isnad and matn with an example chain; explain why tests were needed; describe the isnad tests, contrasting al-Bukhari's and Muslim's conditions; mention biographical dictionaries; describe the matn tests; and finish with the grades from sahih to mawdu'.
caption: Define, explain why, test the chain, test the text, then grade.
